analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes and home-care providers from forcing Medicare and Medicaid patients into pre-dispute arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in committee with 6 cosponsors until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Nursing homes often require residents to sign an arbitration agreement when they are admitted, before any dispute exists. That means if a resident is later injured, abused, or neglected, the family cannot take the facility to court in front of a jury; the case goes to a private arbitrator chosen under industry-favored rules. This bill would prohibit those agreements for Medicare and Medicaid nursing facilities, home- and community-based services, and home health care, and would nullify existing ones. It was referred to two committees, then to a subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid nursing home residents, people receiving home health or home- and community-based care, and their families, who keep the right to sue in court over abuse, neglect, or injury rather than being locked into private arbitration signed at admission.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home and home-care patients and families

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars skilled nursing facilities and nursing facilities from requiring, soliciting, or accepting pre-dispute arbitration agreements from residents and declares such agreements invalid and unenforceable [S2][S3].
The same ban applies to providers of home- and community-based services and home health care under Medicaid, covering the provider and any employee, agent, or affiliate [S2][S3].
It nullifies existing agreements, whether signed before or after the law's effective date, and gives a court, not an arbitrator, the power to decide how the ban applies [S3].
It takes effect on the date of enactment, ending the common practice of presenting residents or their families with an arbitration clause at admission, often at a moment of crisis [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators, home care providers, and their insurers, who would lose a tool that limits their exposure to jury trials and potentially larger verdicts in abuse and neglect cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and their insurers

drawbacks.text: Industry and arbitration supporters argue arbitration is faster and cheaper for families than litigation, and that eliminating it would raise facilities' insurance and legal costs, which could be passed on to care costs.
The bill voids arbitration agreements already signed, including those agreed to voluntarily, raising retroactivity and fairness questions for contracts made under the law as it stood.
The ban covers only Medicare and Medicaid programs, so arbitration agreements could still be used in some care settings outside those programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For residents of the affected facilities, the benefit is concrete: the right to a day in court when abuse or neglect occurs, at the moment of harm, instead of a clause signed at admission. The costs fall on facilities through higher litigation exposure, and families may in some cases wait longer or spend more than arbitration would take. On balance the bill protects a group that often has no realistic ability to negotiate admission paperwork, and the industry-side costs are the intended effect of restoring liability.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on December 5, 2019, with Rep. Jan Schakowsky, and it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S3][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 116th Congress [S5].
It drew 6 cosponsors, all House Democrats, out of 231 in the chamber, and never came to a vote in either chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators and home care providers keep the ability to require residents to sign away their right to a jury trial before any dispute exists, limiting their liability for abuse and neglect claims.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators and their insurers

against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed restrictions on mandatory arbitration in nursing facilities, which limit its liability for abuse and neglect claims.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record.

industries.industry: Nursing home operators (skilled nursing and Medicaid nursing facilities)
industries.note: The bill removes their ability to require residents to sign arbitration clauses at admission, which would expose them to jury trials over abuse and neglect claims. Arbitration clauses protect the facility's interest in avoiding larger jury verdicts, which runs directly against residents' interest in their day in court.

industries.industry: Home health and home- and community-based care providers
industries.note: The bill bars these providers and their affiliates from enforcing pre-dispute arbitration against patients receiving Medicaid-covered home care.
The bill eliminates a stream of nursing home and home care arbitration business by making the underlying agreements void.
